item.title: Fieldkey is live on Google Play: identify plants, rocks and coins offline
item.description: Fieldkey is a new Android app from Hartmann Studios that identifies plants, rocks, minerals and US coins right on your phone, with no account, no upload and no internet needed. Now free on Google Play.
item.content:encoded:
Snap it. Know it.

Fieldkey, a new Android app from Hartmann Studios, is now live on Google Play. It identifies plants, rocks, minerals and US coins right on your phone, with no account, no upload and no internet needed.

Three modes in one app

  • Plants: about 2,100 wild and garden species, plus 100 popular houseplants and garden plants, with light, water and pet-safety notes.
  • Rocks: about 130 rocks, minerals, crystals and gemstones, with hardness, streak, crystal system and simple tests you can do at home.
  • Coins: 22 US coin types. Fieldkey also reads the year and mint mark from your photo and flags silver content and well-known key dates.

Honest by design

Every result shows how confident the model is and the next-best matches. When it is not sure, it says so and asks for another angle.

Coin values are only ever given as an estimated range, so check a dealer before you sell anything. Plant safety notes are general information, not medical or veterinary advice. Never eat a plant or mushroom because an app said so.

Private and offline

All identification runs on your phone. Your photos never leave the device. There is no account and no analytics, and it works without a connection.

You can save finds to your collection with the photo, date and your own notes, and share a find card with friends.

Free and Pro

The free version gives you 3 identifications a day, plus one more by watching a short video. Pro removes the limit and the ads and adds collection export. It comes as a monthly or yearly subscription (with a free trial) or a one-time lifetime purchase.

Fieldkey is built on open models and open data: the Google AIY plant classifier, photos from iNaturalist and Wikimedia Commons contributors, and descriptions from Wikipedia and Wikidata.

Get it

Fieldkey is free on Google Play: Fieldkey: Plant Rock Coin ID. More details are on the app's site: https://chartmann1590.github.io/fieldkey-site/.

item.title: AuraCast Weather: your forecast as an on-device spoken briefing
item.description: AuraCast Weather turns your forecast into a spoken briefing made on your phone, with live radar, alerts, widgets and offline translation.
item.content:encoded:
Checking the weather usually means reading a screen of icons and numbers while you are trying to get out the door. AuraCast Weather adds another option: a short spoken briefing, written by an AI model on your phone and read aloud in a natural voice, so you can hear the day ahead while you get ready.

What it does

  • Forecasts. Current conditions, a 48-hour hourly forecast and a 5-day forecast, using Open-Meteo and the National Weather Service, with animated weather icons.
  • AI weather podcast. Gemma 4 runs on the device and writes the briefing, then a neural text-to-speech voice reads it aloud. You can pick and preview your favorite voice in Settings.
  • Animated radar. A precipitation radar on a free OpenStreetMap base map, with play, pause and scrub over a 40-minute loop.
  • Translation. On-device translation into 58 languages. The language models download once and then work offline.
  • Alerts. Severe-weather alerts and daily briefing notifications.
  • Everyday touches. Light and dark Material 3 themes, widgets, and support for phones and tablets.

How the briefing is made

The interesting part is where the AI runs. The app fetches the forecast numbers, then hands them to a local model on your phone, which turns them into a natural spoken report. According to the listing, there are no cloud AI calls for the report itself, and the AI report never leaves your device.

That means the briefing does not depend on a remote AI service, and nothing about your morning routine is sent to one. It does still need the internet for the forecast data and radar images.

A hands-free morning

  1. Pick a voice in Settings and preview it.
  2. Turn on the daily briefing notification.
  3. Add a widget to your home screen for a quick glance.
  4. Leave severe-weather alerts on.
  5. If you prefer another language, download its translation model once.

Privacy

The listing spells out the network use:

  • The only network calls are for fetching the forecast and radar imagery.
  • Crash diagnostics use an anonymous install ID.
  • Ads follow Google's Advertising ID policies, with a consent prompt where required.
  • No account is required.

Good to know

  • AuraCast Weather is free to download and contains ads.
  • No account is needed.
  • The app is open source; the listing links to its code repository.
  • The forecast sources include the National Weather Service, so some data is specific to the United States.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Weather category.

Is it for you?

  • You would rather hear the forecast than read it.
  • You want the AI part to run on your own phone, not in the cloud.
  • You check the radar before heading out.
  • You want severe-weather alerts and a home screen widget.
  • You like apps that publish their source code.

Get AuraCast Weather on Google Play

item.title: How Shape & Shade maps a face on your phone
item.description: A look under the hood: 478 face points from an on-device model, four measurements, plain-math shape matching, and why the app shows the lines instead of a verdict.
item.content:encoded:
Shape & Shade answers one question, "what's my face shape?", without sending your face anywhere. Here's how it does that on the phone.

Step 1: find the face points

The app runs Google's MediaPipe Face Landmarker on the device (the float16 model, about 3.8 MB, bundled in the app). It returns 478 three-dimensional points: the outline of the face, the brows, eyes, irises, nose, lips and jaw. This is the only "AI" in the face-shape scan. Everything after it is ordinary arithmetic.

Step 2: measure

From those points the app takes four measurements:

  • Forehead width, across the top of the face
  • Cheekbone width, the widest line across the cheekbones
  • Jaw width, across the angles of the jaw
  • Face length, from the hairline area to the chin

It also looks at how sharp or soft the jawline is and how narrow the chin is. Dividing these gives ratios that don't depend on how far you held the phone: length to width, forehead to jaw, jaw to cheekbones.

Step 3: match, and say how sure

Each of the six shapes (oval, round, square, heart, diamond, oblong) has a reference set of ratios. The app measures how close your ratios are to each one. The closest is your shape. If the runner-up is nearly as close, the result says so ("between heart and oval") instead of pretending to be sure. That's why the result is called an estimate from your measurements.

Step 4: show the work

The result screen draws the measurement lines on your photo and lists the reasons in plain words, for example "Your forehead is wider than your jaw" or "Your jawline is softly curved". You can check it yourself.

What stays on the phone

The model, the photo, the points and the result. There's no account and nothing is uploaded. Pro's Color Season scan works the same way: a second on-device model (MediaPipe's selfie segmenter) separates skin, hair and clothes, and the colors are compared in CIELAB space with a white sheet of paper for white balance. Color season is for fun and style ideas.

What it doesn't do

No beauty scores, and no guessing at age, ethnicity or gender. The guides suggest; they don't judge.

Shape & Shade is free on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.charles.shapeshade.

item.title: CruiseLoom: an offline-first planner for cruise days and ports
item.description: CruiseLoom keeps your cruise itinerary, port weather and route map on your phone, with nearby chat for your group over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct.
item.content:encoded:
A cruise is a strange place to rely on your phone. Internet at sea can be slow, expensive or missing, your plans change port by port, and your group scatters across a ship the size of a small town. CruiseLoom is a cruise companion built around that reality: your itinerary works offline, weather is cached for weak connections, and your party can chat nearby without the internet.

What it does

  • Voyage planning. Set your ship and sailing dates, see sea days, port days and upcoming plans at a glance, and add dinners, shows, excursions and local reminders.
  • Port prep. Search and organize real port stops, check current conditions and a seven-day forecast, and cache recent weather for patchy connections.
  • Route map. View your itinerary on a route map built on OpenStreetMap.
  • Deck plans. Download optional ship-deck schematics for supported ships.
  • Nearby group chat. Add shipmates with a QR code generated on your phone, then chat over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct using broadcast or private messages.
  • Guest chat. Host temporary guest Wi-Fi chat for companions who do not have the app.

Before you sail

  1. Enter your ship and sailing dates.
  2. Add your port stops and check each one's forecast.
  3. Put dinners, shows and excursions on the right days, with reminders.
  4. Download the deck schematics if your ship is supported.
  5. Open the app with a connection before boarding so recent weather is cached.

Once that is done, the core itinerary planning remains useful offline, which is the point on days when the ship's internet is not cooperating.

Keeping the group together

The chat feature does not depend on the ship's internet. Shipmates scan a locally generated QR code to join, and messages travel directly between nearby phones over Bluetooth and Wi-Fi Direct. You can send a message to everyone or privately to one person. For a companion without the app, you can host a temporary guest Wi-Fi chat instead.

Where your data lives

The listing is clear about this: CruiseLoom stores cruise plans and chat history locally on your device, and Android cloud backup is disabled. Online services are used only for features such as weather, maps, optional deck downloads, diagnostics and advertising, as explained in the app's privacy policy. Because backup is off, plans live only on that phone.

Good to know

  • CruiseLoom is free to download and contains ads.
  • Some features ask for optional permissions: camera, nearby devices, location or notifications.
  • CruiseLoom is an independent app and is not affiliated with or endorsed by any cruise line.
  • Deck schematics are only available for supported ships.
  • It is rated Teen, in the Travel and Local category.

Is it for you?

  • You have a cruise coming up and want every day's plan in one place.
  • You expect weak or pricey internet at sea and need things to work offline.
  • You travel with a group and want a way to message without ship Wi-Fi.
  • You like keeping your plans on your own device rather than in a cloud account.

Get CruiseLoom on Google Play

item.title: CruiseWatch: get alerted when your booked cruise fare drops
item.description: CruiseWatch tracks the public fare on a cruise you already booked and alerts you when it drops, with the claim steps and deadline for your line.
item.content:encoded:
Booking a cruise is usually not the end of the price story. Fares keep moving after you pay your deposit, and many cruise lines will refund the difference or give onboard credit if the price drops before your final payment date. The catch: you have to notice the drop and ask before the window closes. CruiseWatch does the noticing.

What it does

  • Watches your booked cruise. Add your ship, sail date and cabin category, and CruiseWatch checks the public fare.
  • Covers five lines. Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Carnival, Princess and Norwegian.
  • Instant push alerts. When a lower fare appears, you get the new price and how much you are owed.
  • Exact next steps. Each alert shows the cruise line's phone number, a ready-to-read script, and your claim deadline, based on that line's price-drop or "Best Price Guarantee" policy.
  • On-device AI refund assistant. Ask questions about a specific alert and get step-by-step help claiming a refund or onboard credit.
  • Wear OS companion. Installed automatically with the phone app, it shows price-drop alerts and your claim history on your watch.
  • Home screen widget. Check status at a glance.

How a claim works

The flow is short:

  1. Add each cruise you have already booked: ship, sail date and cabin category.
  2. Let CruiseWatch watch the public pricing.
  3. When an alert arrives, read the new price and the amount you are owed.
  4. Call the number shown in the alert, using the script provided.
  5. Do it before the claim deadline in the alert.

The script and deadline are the useful part. Policies differ by line, and the app pulls the steps from each line's own price-drop policy instead of leaving you to search for the terms.

Privacy

The AI refund assistant runs entirely on your device and works fully offline, and the listing states that your booking details never leave your phone when you use it.

Good to know

  • CruiseWatch is free to use with ads, and there is an optional ad-free monthly subscription.
  • It only works with cruises already booked on Royal Caribbean, Celebrity, Carnival, Princess or Norwegian.
  • CruiseWatch is an independent tool and is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by any cruise line.
  • Pricing and policy information is provided for reference only. Always confirm current terms directly with your cruise line before requesting a refund; a refund or credit is never guaranteed by the app.
  • Most lines only honor a drop before your final payment date, so add your cruise as soon as you book.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Travel and Local category.

Is it for you?

  • You have a cruise booked with one of the five supported lines.
  • Your final payment date has not passed yet.
  • You would rather get a push alert than check fares by hand every week.
  • You want the phone number, script and deadline ready when a drop happens.
  • You wear a Wear OS watch and like alerts on your wrist.

Get CruiseWatch: Fare Drop Alerts on Google Play

item.title: Real HTTPS for your homelab without opening a single port
item.description: Self-signed warnings, a private CA nobody can install, or port forwarding? None of them. Here is the fix from Containers Without the Chaos - Caddy, a DNS-01 wildcard certificate and split DNS, so every internal app gets a real padlock and nothing is exposed.
item.content:encoded:
You want https://notes.home.example.com to open with a padlock and no warning on every device in the house, including the phones of guests you will never install a certificate on. And you want it without opening a single port to the internet. Containers Without the Chaos covers this in two chapters: a reverse proxy done right, then real HTTPS for internal names.

The trap: three half-solutions

There are three common ways people try this, and each one fails in its own way:

  • Self-signed certificates. Every browser warns, every family member learns to click "continue anyway", and that habit is the real security problem.
  • A private certificate authority. It works, but every device needs the CA installed, and many phones, TVs and apps make that hard.
  • Port forwarding 80 and 443 so the normal HTTP challenge works. Now your internal apps are reachable from the internet, which is the opposite of the goal.

The fix: the DNS-01 challenge

To issue a certificate, a public certificate authority such as Let's Encrypt has to check that you control the name. With the DNS challenge, the CA does an authoritative DNS lookup for a special TXT record, and if it sees the expected value, it issues the certificate. No open ports, and the server asking for the certificate never has to be reachable from outside.

You need two things:

  1. A real domain you own, with its DNS hosted at a provider that has an API and a Caddy DNS module (Cloudflare and many others have one; the module list is on caddyserver.com/download).
  2. An API token that lets Caddy create and delete TXT records in that zone.

Names under .local, .internal and .home.arpa cannot get publicly trusted certificates. Use a subdomain of a real domain you own, such as home.example.com.

One wildcard for everything

Instead of one certificate per app, ask for one wildcard: *.home.example.com. It covers notes.home.example.com, photos.home.example.com and anything you add later. Wildcards require the DNS challenge, and a certificate may have only one wildcard, as the left-most label.

There is a privacy bonus. Certificates are published in public Certificate Transparency logs, so per-app certificates would list every internal app name for anyone to read. A wildcard reveals only *.home.example.com.

Build Caddy with a DNS module

The standard Caddy image does not include DNS provider modules, so build your own with the official builder image and xcaddy. Create /srv/stacks/proxy/Dockerfile (Cloudflare shown; use your provider's module):

FROM caddy:2.11-builder AS builder
RUN xcaddy build \
    --with github.com/caddy-dns/cloudflare

FROM caddy:2.11
COPY --from=builder /usr/bin/caddy /usr/bin/caddy

Point the proxy stack at it instead of the plain image. Ports, volumes and networks stay as in the proxy chapter (80, 443 and 443/udp; the ./conf folder mounted at /etc/caddy; ./data for certificates; the external proxy network):

services:
  caddy:
    build: .
    image: local/caddy-dns:2.11
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file: ./caddy.env

Build, start and confirm the module is in:

docker compose build --pull
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec caddy caddy list-modules | grep dns

The API token

Create a token at your DNS provider that can edit DNS records in this one zone and nothing else. Put it in caddy.env, readable only by you, and keep the file out of Git:

CF_API_TOKEN=paste-the-token-here
chmod 600 /srv/stacks/proxy/caddy.env

That token can change DNS for your whole domain. Scope it to the single zone and to DNS edit only. If it leaks, revoke it at the provider and create a new one.

The wildcard Caddyfile

Put every internal site inside one wildcard site block and pick the app with a host matcher. This is the pattern from Caddy's "Common Caddyfile Patterns" page:

*.home.example.com {
    tls {
        dns cloudflare {env.CF_API_TOKEN}
    }

    @notes host notes.home.example.com
    handle @notes {
        reverse_proxy notes:8080
    }

    @photos host photos.home.example.com
    handle @photos {
        reverse_proxy photos:2283
    }

    handle {
        abort
    }
}

The last handle block catches any name you have not defined and closes the connection, so a typo does not land on some other app. Since Caddy 2.10, separate site blocks per app also use an automated wildcard certificate; the single block just keeps the tls settings in one place.

Reload without downtime and watch for the certificate:

docker compose exec -w /etc/caddy caddy caddy reload
docker compose logs caddy | grep -i -E "certificate|obtain"

While testing, add acme_ca https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory inside the tls block. Staging certificates are not trusted by browsers, but staging has much looser rate limits. Remove the line once it works. And never delete ./data to "start fresh": it holds every certificate Caddy has obtained, and certificate authorities enforce rate limits.

Split DNS: names that only exist at home

The certificate proves the names are yours. Now your network has to answer them. Your public DNS zone does not need any record for *.home.example.com at all; only your local resolver answers it, pointing every name at the Docker VM.

On OPNsense with Unbound, add one host override: host *, domain home.example.com, address 192.168.20.10. If your resolver does not support wildcard overrides, add one override per app. In plain Unbound configuration it looks like this:

server:
  local-zone: "home.example.com." redirect
  local-data: "home.example.com. 300 IN A 192.168.20.10"

Check from a laptop on the LAN:

dig +short notes.home.example.com
# 192.168.20.10
curl -I https://notes.home.example.com

If a name resolves on the Docker VM but not on a laptop, suspect DNS rebinding protection. Some resolvers and routers refuse answers that point a public domain at a private address. Check the resolver's rebind settings and allow your internal domain.

Away from home

Nothing here is reachable from the internet, by design. To use these names away from home, connect to your network over WireGuard or Tailscale and make sure the VPN hands out your local resolver. The same names and the same certificate then work everywhere.

Checklist

  • A subdomain of a real domain you own, never .local, .internal or .home.arpa
  • Caddy built with your DNS provider's module, and caddy list-modules | grep dns shows it
  • An API token scoped to one zone and DNS edit only, in caddy.env with chmod 600, kept out of Git
  • One *.home.example.com block with a host matcher per app and a final handle { abort }
  • Staging CA while testing, removed once the certificate arrives; ./data kept and backed up
  • A local DNS override pointing *.home.example.com at the Docker VM, nothing in the public zone
  • Rebind protection allows your internal domain; dig and curl -I pass from a laptop
  • Remote access through WireGuard or Tailscale, handing out your local resolver
  • No ports 80 or 443 forwarded from the internet

Go deeper: Containers Without the Chaos

item.title: Looki L1 mount v9: snug holder + slide-in collar clips (free STL)
item.description: Version 9 of the free 3D-printed Looki L1 wearable camera mount. A snug holder sized for the bare camera and two collar clips that slide in on dovetail rails and click locked. STL downloads, the exact ABS print settings and the real print timelapse.
item.content:encoded:
The free Looki L1 mount is on version 9, and this is the one to print now. It has a new holder that fits the bare camera snugly and two new collar clips (thick and thin) that slide into the back of the holder on full-width dovetail rails and click locked with a small button.

What changed from the last version

  • Holder: the older pocket was sized for the Looki wearing its silicone case, so the bare camera had about 2.4 mm of play on each side. The v9 pocket is the bare Looki plus 0.25 mm per side, with four small snap bumps (0.6 mm over the edge, just above the widest rim) that hold it in. The lens, button and back windows are unchanged.
  • Clips: the old clips only had a dovetail on one side and the tongue stopped half way, so they could pop out. The v9 clips slide in sideways, from the right. That way both rails, top and bottom, are part of the clip's side profile, so they print cleanly and run the clip's full width.
  • Lock: a 1.3 mm flex beam under the rails carries a small button that clicks into a 4.2 mm hole in the holder. The weight hangs on the rails, not on the button.
  • The safety lanyard frame is not part of this release. It's coming in a later update.

Printed and assembled

These photos are the real v9 parts, printed in black ABS.

Downloads

  • looki_v9_holder.stl (964 KB): the holder the Looki snaps into
  • looki_v9_clip_thick.stl (98 KB): the thick collar clip, 32 mm wide
  • looki_v9_clip_thin.stl (101 KB): the thin collar clip, 26 mm wide
  • looki_v9_abs_profile.ini: the PrusaSlicer profile the parts in the photos were printed with
  • Everything as one zip

Also on Printables, where the older v4 files are still available too. License: CC BY 4.0, Charles Hartmann / Homelab the Right Way.

How the clip goes on and comes off

  1. Slide the clip into the channel on the back of the holder from the right side. The rails guide it, and the closed left end is the stop.
  2. Push until the button clicks into the hole in the holder.
  3. To take it off, press the thumb tab toward the shirt and slide the clip out to the right. With the Looki out, you can also push the button from the inside.

Pick the thick or the thin clip, whichever fits your collar better.

Print settings

What the parts in the photos were printed with:

  • Material: ABS, 240 C nozzle and 100 C bed.
  • Layers: 0.2 mm with a 0.4 mm nozzle, 4 perimeters, 40% gyroid infill. No supports.
  • Raft: an easy-peel raft, 3 raft layers with a 0.3 mm contact gap and no raft expansion. It keeps the ABS flat and comes off clean.
  • Orientation: print as exported. The clips print on their side, so the layer lines run around the bend and the arm flexes instead of snapping.
  • Time: the plate in the timelapse (the holder, both clips and the lanyard frame that isn't released yet) took 8 h 22 min.

The timelapse at the top of this page is the real v9 plate printing, straight off the OctoPrint camera.

Fit notes

The Looki outline is based on the camera's official 50.53 x 48.02 mm size. If the holder is too tight or too loose on yours, or a clip is too stiff or too loose on the rails, leave a comment on the Printables page saying which part.

The original v4 cradle and clip, with the screw-on design, are still written up in the first Looki mount post.

Not affiliated with Looki. The Looki L1 is a product of looki.ai; this is an independent, free accessory. The model was designed with AI help and printed and tested on a real printer.

item.title: CrowdTransit: live bus and train stops with community reviews
item.description: CrowdTransit finds bus and train stops, shows real-time arrivals and alerts, and adds commuter reviews of stops and routes. No account needed.
item.content:encoded:
A transit schedule tells you when the bus should come. It does not tell you that the stop has no shelter, that the platform is hard to reach with a stroller, or that a route has been running late all week. CrowdTransit combines both: live transit data for bus and train stops, plus reviews from the people who actually ride them.

What it does

  • Live transit data. Real-time bus and train tracking, upcoming arrivals at a stop, route information and maps, and service alerts and delays.
  • Community reviews. Read reviews of stops and routes, rate your own experience, and see safety and accessibility ratings.
  • Quick search. Find a stop by its stop number or by address, and save your favorite stops.
  • Offline stop lists. Keep a list of stops for your area available without a connection.
  • Nationwide coverage. The listing says it works in cities across the country, on urban and rural routes, with coverage that keeps expanding.
  • No account. You can use it without signing up.

How it works

CrowdTransit is described as community-powered. The schedules and real-time information come from open data sources, and riders add the part official feeds leave out: reviews and ratings for the stops and routes they use. Coverage itself is partly community-contributed, which is how the listing explains its reach into rural routes as well as big cities.

That makes the app more useful the more people use it. Every rating you leave helps the next commuter decide which stop to walk to, or whether a route is worth the wait.

Getting set up for your commute

  1. Search for your usual stop by its number or the street address.
  2. Save it, and any other stops you use, as favorites.
  3. Check upcoming arrivals before you leave, and watch for service alerts or delays on your route.
  4. Save the offline stop list for your area, so you can still look up stops with a weak signal.
  5. After a ride, leave a quick rating so others know what to expect.

The ratings worth reading

Two kinds of rating stand out for planning:

  • Safety ratings help when you are waiting somewhere late or in an unfamiliar area.
  • Accessibility ratings help when you are traveling with a wheelchair, a stroller, heavy bags or anyone who cannot manage stairs.

Neither replaces official information from your transit agency, but both answer questions a timetable never will.

Good to know

  • CrowdTransit is free to download, and the listing describes it as free with no subscriptions.
  • Google Play's listing labels the app as containing ads and offering in-app purchases.
  • No account is required.
  • It is rated Teen, in the Maps and Navigation category.
  • Coverage depends on available data and community contributions, so check that your area is covered.

Is it for you?

  • You ride buses or trains and want live arrivals and delay alerts in one place.
  • You care about how safe or accessible a stop is, not only when the bus comes.
  • You like being able to rate stops and routes and help other riders.
  • You want to look up stops without creating an account.

Get CrowdTransit: Bus & Train on Google Play

item.title: Promtail is dead: ship your homelab logs to Loki with Grafana Alloy
item.description: Promtail reached end of life on March 2, 2026. Here is the replacement pipeline from Watch Your Homelab, with Loki 3.7, retention that actually deletes, Grafana Alloy reading the journal and Docker logs, and LogQL queries worth saving.
item.content:encoded:
Metrics tell you that something changed. Logs tell you why. Watch Your Homelab gives logs their own chapter because the usual homelab approach only works until the day you actually need it.

The trap: SSH, journalctl, and a dead agent

The default homelab log strategy is SSH and journalctl, one machine at a time, after the fact. By the time you look, the container was recreated and its logs went with it, or the journal on a small root disk has already rotated.

The second trap is building a log stack from an old tutorial. Many of them still use Promtail, which reached end of life on March 2, 2026. Grafana's documentation states that it receives no further updates and that future development happens in Grafana Alloy. New setups should start with Alloy.

How the pieces fit

  • Loki stores logs. Unlike a full-text search engine, it indexes only a small set of labels (host, unit, container) and stores the log lines compressed in chunks. That keeps it light enough for a homelab.
  • Alloy is the agent. It reads the systemd journal and Docker's container logs on each host, attaches labels, and pushes the lines to Loki.
  • Grafana queries Loki with LogQL, from the same place that shows your dashboards.

Run Loki with retention switched on

At the time the book was written (October 2026), Loki is at 3.7. A single Loki process with local filesystem storage is the right size for a homelab. This config is based on the project's own local example, with retention turned on:

# /opt/stacks/logs/loki/config.yaml
auth_enabled: false

server:
  http_listen_port: 3100

common:
  instance_addr: 127.0.0.1
  path_prefix: /loki
  storage:
    filesystem:
      chunks_directory: /loki/chunks
      rules_directory: /loki/rules
  replication_factor: 1
  ring:
    kvstore:
      store: inmemory

schema_config:
  configs:
    - from: 2026-10-01
      store: tsdb
      object_store: filesystem
      schema: v13
      index:
        prefix: index_
        period: 24h

compactor:
  working_directory: /loki/compactor
  retention_enabled: true
  delete_request_store: filesystem

limits_config:
  retention_period: 30d

analytics:
  reporting_enabled: false
# /opt/stacks/logs/compose.yaml
services:
  loki:
    image: grafana/loki:3.7.8
    restart: unless-stopped
    command: ["-config.file=/etc/loki/config.yaml"]
    ports: ["3100:3100"]
    volumes:
      - ./loki/config.yaml:/etc/loki/config.yaml:ro
      - loki-data:/loki
volumes:
  loki-data:

Retention is the part people get wrong. In Loki, the compactor does the deleting, and Loki's documentation is explicit on three points:

  1. retention_enabled must be true. Otherwise the compactor only compacts.
  2. delete_request_store must be set when retention is on.
  3. Retention needs the 24-hour index period used in the schema above.

retention_period in limits_config then applies to every log stream. The last block turns off Loki's anonymous usage reporting, which the example config leaves on by default.

Install Alloy on each host

Alloy runs as a native service, which makes reading the journal straightforward. These steps follow Grafana's Debian instructions (Alloy 1.20 when the book was written). Run them on the Proxmox host and on each Docker host:

apt install gpg
mkdir -p /etc/apt/keyrings
wget -O /etc/apt/keyrings/grafana.asc https://apt.grafana.com/gpg-full.key
chmod 644 /etc/apt/keyrings/grafana.asc
echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/grafana.asc] \
https://apt.grafana.com stable main" > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/grafana.list
apt-get update && apt-get install alloy
usermod -aG adm,systemd-journal alloy

Don't skip the last line. Alloy's documentation warns that without membership in adm and systemd-journal, the journal source starts without an error and collects nothing. That's a silent failure, the worst kind for a logging system.

On Docker hosts, also add the alloy user to the docker group so it can read container logs through the socket. That comes with a caveat: access to the Docker socket is full control of Docker on that host.

The Alloy config

The config lives in /etc/alloy/config.alloy. It's a set of components wired together: sources forward to a writer. This is the book's example for a Docker host named docker1, with Loki on the monitoring guest at 192.168.10.20:

// /etc/alloy/config.alloy on docker1
loki.write "default" {
  endpoint {
    url = "http://192.168.10.20:3100/loki/api/v1/push"
  }
}

// systemd journal, with unit and level as labels
loki.relabel "journal" {
  forward_to = []
  rule {
    source_labels = ["__journal__systemd_unit"]
    target_label  = "unit"
  }
  rule {
    source_labels = ["__journal_priority_keyword"]
    target_label  = "level"
  }
}

loki.source.journal "host" {
  forward_to    = [loki.write.default.receiver]
  relabel_rules = loki.relabel.journal.rules
  labels        = {host = "docker1", job = "journal"}
}

// Docker containers, labelled by container name
discovery.docker "local" {
  host = "unix:///var/run/docker.sock"
}

discovery.relabel "containers" {
  targets = discovery.docker.local.targets
  rule {
    source_labels = ["__meta_docker_container_name"]
    regex         = "/(.*)"
    target_label  = "container"
  }
}

loki.source.docker "containers" {
  host       = "unix:///var/run/docker.sock"
  targets    = discovery.relabel.containers.output
  forward_to = [loki.write.default.receiver]
  labels     = {host = "docker1", job = "docker"}
}

On the Proxmox host, keep the loki.write and journal blocks and drop the Docker ones. The journal there carries pvedaemon, pveproxy, pvestatd, backup jobs and the kernel. Restart with systemctl restart alloy and check it with systemctl status alloy. When started with a listen address, Alloy also serves a debugging UI on port 12345 that shows each component and whether it's healthy.

Labels: few and boring

Loki is fast because its index is small. Every distinct combination of label values creates a new stream, and too many streams make Loki slow and heavy. Keep labels to things with only a handful of values that you filter by: host, job, unit, container, level. Never turn request IDs, user names, IP addresses or full paths into labels. Search for those in the log line instead.

Four LogQL queries worth saving

In Grafana, open Explore, pick the Loki data source, start with a label selector, then filter lines:

{host="pve1", unit="pvedaemon.service"}
{job="docker", container="immich_server"} |= "error"
{job="journal", level=~"err|crit|alert|emerg"}
sum by (host) (count_over_time({level="err"}[1h]))

In order, these show:

  1. The Proxmox API daemon's log.
  2. Only the lines containing "error" from one container.
  3. Every high-priority journal line across the lab.
  4. Errors per host per hour. This turns logs into a metric, and it makes a good panel on an overview dashboard.

Grafana alert rules can run LogQL too. The book's advice is to use that sparingly, for lines that only appear when something is wrong, like a backup job's failure message or repeated authentication failures on a service you expose.

Don't forget the local logs

Loki gives you a searchable copy, but Docker still keeps container logs on the host. With the default json-file logging driver, they grow without limit unless you configure them. Set limits in /etc/docker/daemon.json on each Docker host and restart Docker. Existing containers pick up the change when they're recreated.

{
    "log-driver": "json-file",
    "log-opts": { "max-size": "10m", "max-file": "3" }
}

Cap the journal too: set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf, then run systemctl restart systemd-journald. Loki is now the long memory, so local logs only need to cover a few days.

Checklist

  • No Promtail in new setups: Alloy on every host
  • Loki 3.7 with retention_enabled: true, delete_request_store set, a 24h index period and retention_period: 30d
  • The alloy user in adm and systemd-journal (plus docker on Docker hosts)
  • Journal on every host, container logs on every Docker host, systemctl status alloy clean
  • Labels limited to host, job, unit, container and level
  • The four LogQL queries saved, with the errors-per-host query as a dashboard panel
  • Docker log rotation in daemon.json and SystemMaxUse=500M for the journal

item.title: Podcast, episode 2: Blue by Sunday — lock down your home network
item.description: Episode 2 of the Homelab the Right Way Podcast, 42 minutes with three AI hosts on zones, VLANs, OPNsense rules that mean something, the IoT discovery trap that turns the cast button grey, locking yourself out of your own firewall (and WireGuard as the way back in), plus this week's tech news, the LiveCaptionN app and a managed-switch gear break. Player, chapters, sources and links.
item.content:encoded:
Episode 2 is the networking episode. Maya, Sam and Theo work through Lock Down Your Home Network (book 5) from the first question, "which zone is this device in?", to the Saturday-afternoon rule that locks you out of your own firewall. Along the way: this week's real tech news with sources, an app that actually belongs in a networking episode, and a managed switch.

A note on the hosts: Maya, Sam and Theo are fictional AI hosts. Their voices are synthetic, their faces in the clips are generated, and the episode was written with AI and edited by a human. Every technical fact in the episode comes from the Homelab the Right Way books; the news segment cites its sources below.

Meet the hosts (45-second promo)

Maya, Sam and Theo introduce the show in 45 seconds: watch it on YouTube or on Bluesky. New episodes every Sunday, free on podcast apps and YouTube.

Chapters

  • 00:04 — Cold open: the cast button is grey, and welcome
  • 01:49 — New tech this week: TP-Link lawsuits, OPNsense 26.7.7, Home Assistant 2026.10
  • 06:22 — Think in zones, then lock the front door
  • 13:22 — VLANs from the wire up, and rules that mean something
  • 21:36 — IoT that still works: why the cast button goes grey, and the Home Assistant leg
  • 28:29 — App spot: LiveCaptionN, live captions that can run on your own server
  • 30:53 — Gear break: the managed switch
  • 32:13 — Listener question: I locked myself out of my own firewall. How do I never do that again?
  • 39:04 — Merch, the ebooks, and the free weekly email
  • 40:18 — Three takeaways, and where everything lives

New tech this week, with sources (01:49)

Three stories and one quick one, all checked the week of recording. The hosts only say what the sources say.

  • Four more US states sue TP-Link; TP-Link denies the claims. Florida, Iowa, Montana and Nebraska filed consumer-protection suits on October 6 (Texas filed in February). The complaints allege advertised security that was not delivered (quoting the HomeShield page's "covers all security scenarios" against router models that stopped getting updates), an overstated separation from China, and a privacy-policy gap. TP-Link's statement the same day calls the suits "built on false premises", says its US routers are made in Vietnam and that it does not share customer network data with foreign governments. Sources: The Hacker News, Oct 9 and TP-Link's statement, Oct 6. These are allegations; nothing has been decided in court.
  • OPNsense 26.7.7 (October 13). Mostly fixes: the Hyper-V kernel panic fix from 26.7.6 caused segmentation faults for others, now corrected; fixes in the new interface settings API; the iPerf and FRR plugins reworked (read FRR's migration notes before updating); os-ddclient 1.33. Source: the release announcement on the OPNsense forum.
  • Home Assistant 2026.10 "You are here" (October 7; patches Oct 10 and 16). Trigger IDs get a proper UI, a new vector map on OpenStreetMap data with a Map tiles integration that fetches and caches tiles through your own instance, Home Assistant Cloud to be renamed Home Assistant Link in December, and 15 new integrations. Source: the Home Assistant release post.
  • Quick one: Bitwarden switched to a dual-licensing model, per the Self-Host Weekly roundup of October 16; the concern about the "all current features" wording is the newsletter author's, not ours.

What the episode covers, with the articles

Think in zones, then lock the front door (06:22). The flat-network trap, the five zones (trusted, servers, IoT, guest, management; VLAN 10/20/30/40/99 with the VLAN number as the third octet), the downhill rule and the one named uphill exception (Home Assistant into IoT). Then chapter 2 in order: the ADMIN_HOSTS alias, the web interface on HTTPS and management only, an explicit admin pass rule tested before disabling anti-lockout, TOTP two-factor (code then password in the password field, no space), a named admin, SSH by key or off, a console menu password, no UPnP plugin, and nothing administrative on WAN.

  • What a /24 subnet actually means (and how to plan yours)
  • Guest Wi-Fi that can't reach your servers: 5 OPNsense rules, in order

VLANs from the wire up, and rules that mean something (13:22). Access ports vs trunk ports, the 4-byte 802.1Q tag, the two ways VLANs fail (a stripped tag, or a tag that is optional where it must not be), never VLAN 1 for anything you care about, the OPNsense steps (Devices > VLAN, Assignments, DHCP), one SSID per wireless zone. Then rules: they apply where traffic enters, first match wins, anything unmatched is blocked; aliases first; the four-step pattern for every zone; the three IoT rules; log the block rule for a week; IOT_LOCAL_ONLY; and a "why" description on every rule.

IoT that still works (21:36). Why the cast button goes grey (mDNS 224.0.0.251 UDP 5353 and SSDP 239.255.255.250 UDP 1900 do not cross a router), the os-mdns-repeater plugin on TRUSTED and IOT only, narrow call-back rules for Chromecast/AirPlay, the SSDP relay, Home Assistant on a second network card in VLAN 30 (and the patching trade-off), the device-by-device list (ESPHome, MQTT on 1883/8883, printers on 631, cameras), and the NTP/DNS redirect for devices that ignore DHCP.

Listener question: locked out of my own firewall (32:13). The chapter 8 habit (write it down, restore point, one change, test card, keep or roll back), the ladder back in (console restore, snapshot rollback, set-interface-IP to plain HTTP, reinstall + config.xml), and chapter 6, WireGuard: the carrier-grade NAT check (100.64.0.0/10), key pairs instead of passwords, the home-wg instance on UDP 51820 with 10.99.0.1/24, one peer per device with its own /32, dynamic DNS as the endpoint, split vs full tunnel (AllowedIPs), the single WAN rule, and wg show for the handshake.

App spot (28:29)

LiveCaptionN on Google Play: free live captions in a floating window over any app, video or call, from the microphone or internal audio (Android 10+), real-time speech-to-text (Vosk) and translation into 59+ languages. Two modes: on-device (audio never leaves the phone) or self-hosted, pointing the app at your own server running Whisper ASR and LibreTranslate in Docker. Core features are free with ads; optional Ad-Free and Pro upgrades.

Gear mentioned in this episode (30:53)

As an Amazon Associate the show earns from qualifying purchases. These are affiliate links; the price you pay is the same.

  • NETGEAR GS308E 8-port gigabit Plus switch: the example for the book's "managed switch with 802.1Q VLAN support". What to check on any model: per-port tagged/untagged, VLAN 1 removable from ports that don't need it, and a management address you can park on the management VLAN.
  • From episode 1: TP-Link TL-SG105 5-port gigabit switch, unmanaged, still right for a desk.

Merch, books and the newsletter (39:04)

  • Lock Down Your Home Network and the whole series, every book with a free sample chapter.
  • Podcast merch: The Green Check Lies tee, the Go Restore Something hoodie and more.
  • The free weekly email: every Sunday, the week's posts, videos, the episode and one tip, plus a one-page homelab checklist when you join.

item.title: Knightfall: play Stockfish and get coached by on-device AI
item.description: Knightfall pairs the Stockfish chess engine with Gemma 4 coaching, plus online play, a web version, puzzles and rating tracking.
item.content:encoded:
Playing a strong engine is a good way to lose a lot of chess games. It is not always a good way to learn, because the engine never tells you why your move was bad. Knightfall puts a coach next to the engine: you play against Stockfish, and an AI model, Gemma 4, explains your games and suggests where to improve.

What it does

  • Play Stockfish at any difficulty. From beginner to grandmaster level, with adaptive AI that the listing says learns with you.
  • AI coaching. Gemma 4 analyzes your games, gives personalized move suggestions, offers opening and endgame tips, and walks through post-game analysis with explanations. The listing describes this coaching as on-device.
  • More ways to play. Online multiplayer matches, a local two-player mode on one device, and a web version you can play without downloading anything.
  • Progress tracking. Rating history and statistics, win, loss and draw tracking, an opening repertoire builder, and a puzzle mode for tactics training.
  • Custom games. Custom time controls and a tournament mode.
  • Looks. A clean board, multiple themes and piece sets, animations and sound effects, and dark mode.

Engine and coach: two different jobs

Stockfish is a well-known open chess engine: it calculates moves and is very strong at it. A language model like Gemma 4 does something else, which is putting ideas into words. Knightfall uses each for what it is good at. The engine is your opponent at whatever level you set, and the coach turns your finished game into explanations you can read.

A practical loop looks like this:

  1. Play a game against Stockfish at a level where you win some and lose some.
  2. Open the post-game analysis and read the explanations for the moves that mattered.
  3. Look at the opening and endgame tips that come out of your games.
  4. Spend a few minutes in puzzle mode to drill tactics.
  5. Watch your rating history to see whether it is working.

Playing across devices

The Android app has the full feature set, and there is a web version for desktop. The listing mentions cloud save across devices, so you can move between phone and computer. When you want a human opponent, there is online multiplayer, or local two-player mode for passing one phone across a table.

Good to know

  • Knightfall is free to download, described as free with optional premium.
  • Google Play marks the app as containing ads.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Strategy games category.
  • Online multiplayer and cloud save need a connection; the listing describes play as online, offline or on the web.

Is it for you?

  • You play engines but want to understand your mistakes, not just see them.
  • You want one app for engine games, puzzles and online matches.
  • You like tracking your rating and building an opening repertoire.
  • You switch between your phone and a desktop browser.

Get Knightfall: AI Chess Coach on Google Play

item.title: Stop clicking through the installer: one cloud-init golden image for every Proxmox VM
item.description: Build one Debian 13 cloud-image template in Proxmox with qm create and cloud-init (user, SSH key, network, guest agent), then clone it for every new VM instead of running an installer.
item.content:encoded:
Every new VM that starts with an ISO and a click-through installer is a little different from the last one. A different username here, a forgotten SSH key there, a typo in a static address. Automate Your Homelab starts its rebuildable lab somewhere else: one template made from a distribution's official cloud image, cloned for every VM, with cloud-init filling in the personal details on first boot.

Cloud images are small, minimal installs built to be configured on first boot by cloud-init, which reads its settings from a little drive that Proxmox attaches to the VM. That is how a fresh clone wakes up with the right hostname, your user, your SSH key and its address, without anyone touching a console.

The trap: hand-built VMs that drift

The installer route has two problems. It is slow, and it is not repeatable: nothing records what you typed, so the next VM only matches the last one if you remember every answer. A template built from commands fixes both. A template cannot be started, only cloned, and as the book puts it, that is the point: nobody logs into it, so it never drifts.

Pick the image

The book uses Debian 13 (trixie). Debian publishes cloud images at cloud.debian.org, and at the time of writing (October 2026) the trixie folder holds, among others:

  • debian-13-genericcloud-amd64.qcow2: for cloud and virtual machines, with a smaller set of hardware drivers. This is the one for Proxmox VMs.
  • debian-13-generic-amd64.qcow2: the same system with a wider set of drivers, for odd hardware.

Ubuntu publishes its own cloud images at cloud-images.ubuntu.com, and the commands below are the same for either.

Build the template once

Run these on the Proxmox host. They follow the Proxmox VE Cloud-Init Support documentation; VM ID 9000 and the storage names are examples.

cd /var/lib/vz/template/iso
wget https://cloud.debian.org/images/cloud/trixie/latest/debian-13-genericcloud-amd64.qcow2

qm create 9000 --name debian13-tmpl --memory 2048 \
  --cores 2 --net0 virtio,bridge=vmbr0 \
  --scsihw virtio-scsi-pci --ostype l26 --agent enabled=1

qm set 9000 --scsi0 local-lvm:0,import-from=/var/lib/vz/template/iso/debian-13-genericcloud-amd64.qcow2
qm set 9000 --ide2 local-lvm:cloudinit
qm set 9000 --boot order=scsi0
qm set 9000 --serial0 socket --vga serial0

What each step does:

  • qm create makes an empty VM with a VirtIO network card on bridge vmbr0 and the VirtIO SCSI controller that cloud images expect.
  • import-from copies the downloaded image into a new disk on local-lvm and attaches it as scsi0.
  • --ide2 local-lvm:cloudinit adds the small cloud-init drive. Proxmox writes the user, network and SSH settings onto it.
  • --boot order=scsi0 boots straight from the disk, skipping the CD-ROM check.
  • The serial console is what many cloud images expect as their display. If a particular image does not work with it, switch back to the default display.

Set the defaults every clone inherits

Settings made on the template are inherited by every clone, so put the parts that are the same everywhere here:

qm set 9000 --ciuser admin
qm set 9000 --sshkeys /root/admin_ed25519.pub
qm set 9000 --ipconfig0 ip=dhcp
qm set 9000 --searchdomain home.example.com --nameserver 192.168.20.1

--sshkeys takes a file with one public key per line. Use keys, not --cipassword: the Proxmox documentation itself says passwords are generally not recommended here.

Add the guest agent on first boot

The Debian cloud image does not include the QEMU guest agent, and without it Proxmox (and OpenTofu, later in the book) cannot read the VM's address or shut it down cleanly.

The --cicustom option lets you supply your own files in place of the generated ones. It accepts user, network, meta and vendor files. The catch: replacing user throws away the user and SSH key settings above. Add a vendor file instead, which cloud-init merges with the generated user data.

Custom files must live on a storage that allows the snippets content type. On the default local storage that is /var/lib/vz/snippets/; enable the content type under Datacenter > Storage > local > Content, then create the file:

#cloud-config
# /var/lib/vz/snippets/debian-vendor.yaml
package_update: true
packages:
  - qemu-guest-agent
runcmd:
  - systemctl enable --now qemu-guest-agent

Attach it and check what a clone will receive:

qm set 9000 --cicustom "vendor=local:snippets/debian-vendor.yaml"
qm cloudinit dump 9000 user

The dump command prints the user data Proxmox will generate, which is the quickest way to see what a clone gets. In a cluster, watch out: custom cloud-init files must be available on every node a VM may migrate to, or the VM will not start there. Use shared storage for snippets or copy the file to every node.

Turn it into a template, then clone

qm template 9000

qm clone 9000 120 --name docker01
qm set 120 --ipconfig0 ip=192.168.20.120/24,gw=192.168.20.1
qm disk resize 120 scsi0 20G
qm start 120

After a minute, ssh admin@192.168.20.120 should work with your key. The cloud image's disk is small, which is why the clone's disk is grown with qm disk resize; cloud-init grows the root filesystem to fill it on boot.

By default Proxmox tries to make a linked clone, which depends on the template. For a rebuildable lab the book prefers full clones (pass --full), because the template will be rebuilt whenever a new Debian point release arrives, and full clones do not care.

Keep the template fresh, and keep it in Git

Cloud images are rebuilt regularly with current packages. Every few months, or when a Debian point release comes out, download the new image and create the template again under the same ID, so new VMs start current. Because every step is a command, the rebuild is a script: save the commands as cloud-init/build-template.sh in your lab's repository, and keep the vendor snippet in the repository's cloud-init/ folder too. The copy on the Proxmox host is just a deployment of it.

Checklist

  • Download debian-13-genericcloud-amd64.qcow2, not the generic image, for Proxmox VMs.
  • Create the VM with VirtIO networking, the VirtIO SCSI controller and --agent enabled=1.
  • Import the image with import-from, add the cloudinit drive on ide2, boot from scsi0, serial console on.
  • Set --ciuser, --sshkeys, --ipconfig0 and DNS on the template; skip --cipassword.
  • Add qemu-guest-agent through a vendor snippet, never by replacing user data.
  • Check the result with qm cloudinit dump 9000 user before running qm template 9000.
  • Clone with --full, set the clone's address, grow its disk, start it.
  • Save the build as cloud-init/build-template.sh and rebuild on each Debian point release.

Pantry Tracker, a new Android app from Hartmann Studios, is now live on Google Play. It is an offline-first pantry and expiry tracker: you add groceries, it tells you what to use before it goes bad.

What it does

Private by design

There is no account, and your pantry lives on your phone. Barcode lookups send only the barcode number. Household sharing only happens when you send a file yourself; it never goes through a server. Receipt photos are read on your phone and never uploaded.

item.title: CaptionBurn: burn auto-captions into videos on your phone
item.description: CaptionBurn turns speech into captions with on-device AI, can translate them, and burns them permanently into the video so they show on any player.
item.content:encoded:
Captions make a video watchable with the sound off, and a lot of video is watched exactly that way. The catch is that separate subtitle files often get lost when you share a clip, and many captioning tools want you to upload your footage first. CaptionBurn takes a different route: it generates captions with AI on your phone and burns them directly into the video.

What it does

  • Automatic captions. Speech-to-text for your videos, processed on the device, with support for multiple languages.
  • Burned into the video. The captions become part of the picture itself, so there is no separate caption file and they show up on every video player.
  • Built-in translation. Translate captions into multiple languages, also on the device.
  • Styling. Several subtitle styles, with control over font, size, color, background and position.
  • Workflow helpers. Simple import and export, batch processing, a preview before burning, and one-tap sharing.

Burned-in versus subtitle files

There are two common ways to add captions to a video. One is a separate subtitle track that a player can switch on and off. The other is "burning in", where the text is drawn into the video frames permanently.

CaptionBurn does the second. The trade-off is simple:

Burned-in captionsSeparate subtitle file
Shows on any playerYesOnly if the player supports it
Survives reposting and sharingYesOften lost
Viewer can turn it offNoYes

If your videos end up on social apps or in group chats, burned-in captions are the version that reliably arrives with the clip.

A simple workflow

  1. Import your video.
  2. Let the app generate captions from the speech.
  3. Optionally translate them into another language.
  4. Pick a style and adjust the font, color, size, background and position.
  5. Preview the result before burning.
  6. Burn and share with one tap.

If you have several clips, batch processing lets you work through them without repeating every step by hand.

What stays on your phone

The listing describes CaptionBurn as fully private: all processing happens on the device, no videos are uploaded anywhere, and there is no cloud processing. That also means no waiting for an upload before captions can start, which the listing calls out as part of why processing is fast. The translation step is described as on-device as well.

Good to know

  • CaptionBurn is free to download, described as free with optional premium.
  • Google Play marks the app as containing ads.
  • It is rated Everyone, in the Video Players and Editors category.
  • Because captions are burned in, keep your original file if you might want a version without captions later.

Is it for you?

  • You post short videos and want them to make sense with the sound off.
  • You would rather not upload your footage to a website to get captions.
  • You need captions in more than one language.
  • You want control over how the captions look and where they sit on screen.

item.title: Your homelab has no idea it's down: Uptime Kuma checks that catch real outages
item.description: A ping says the guest is alive, not that the app works. Here is how to set up Uptime Kuma 2 with keyword monitors, sane retries, groups, maintenance windows and a second watcher, so the first person to learn something is down is you.
item.content:encoded:
Who tells you your homelab is down? If the honest answer is "whoever tries to use it first", the book's answer is that Uptime Kuma plus ntfy gets you from silence to useful alerts in an evening. Watch Your Homelab starts its monitoring stack with Uptime Kuma for a simple reason: it answers the first question users ask, "does it work right now?", by doing what a user does, on a timer, and telling you when the answer changes.

The trap: checks that pass while the service is broken

The tempting check is a ping. Ping tells you the guest's network stack is alive. It does not tell you that the web app inside returns a page, that the database behind it answers, or that the certificate has not expired.

The second trap is the default of alerting on the first failed check. One dropped packet at 3 AM and your phone buzzes for a problem that fixed itself two seconds later.

Install it on the monitoring guest

Uptime Kuma 2 is the current major version (2.5 at the time the book was written, October 2026). The book runs it as its own small stack:

# /opt/stacks/uptime-kuma/compose.yaml
services:
  uptime-kuma:
    image: louislam/uptime-kuma:2
    container_name: uptime-kuma
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "3001:3001"
    volumes:
      - ./data:/app/data

Start it with docker compose up -d and open port 3001 on the monitoring guest in a browser. The first visit creates the admin account.

Two details matter here:

  • Keep ./data on local disk. The project states that network file systems such as NFS are not supported for it.
  • Think twice before mounting the Docker socket. Monitoring containers by name needs /var/run/docker.sock, and mounting it gives the container full control of Docker on that host, read-only flag or not. The book's advice: prefer HTTP checks against the service itself, and only add the socket if container state is really what you want to watch.

Pick the monitor type that matches what users experience

Five monitor types cover almost everything in a homelab:

MonitorChecksUse it for
HTTP(s) - KeywordThe page loads and contains a wordWeb apps: Immich, Nextcloud, Home Assistant
HTTP(s)A status code in the accepted rangeAPIs and health endpoints
TCP PortA port accepts a connectionDatabases, SSH, MQTT
DNSA name resolves to the expected recordYour local DNS resolver
PushSomething called a URL in timeBackups, cron jobs, the dead-man switch

The closer a check is to what a user actually does, the more a green light proves.

The keyword monitor is the one to reach for first. A login page that returns HTTP 200 with a "502 Bad Gateway" body from a reverse proxy passes an HTTP check and fails a keyword check. Pick a word that only appears when the app really works, such as the app's name in the page title.

For HTTPS services, open the monitor's advanced settings and turn on the certificate expiry notification. An expiring certificate is the most predictable outage there is, and the check costs nothing.

Retries: ignore the blip, catch the outage

Each monitor has a heartbeat interval, a retry count and a retry interval. A single failed check is marked pending and retried; the monitor only goes down (and notifies) after the first failure plus all retries fail. The book's homelab default:

SettingValueWhy
Heartbeat interval60 sFast enough for a home, light on the services
Retries2Ignores one-off blips
Heartbeat retry interval20 sConfirms a real outage within about a minute
Resend notification if down0 or a few hundredOff, or a reminder every few hours

One blip produces no alert; a real outage produces one alert about a minute later. For slow-by-nature things, like a NAS spinning up its disks, use a longer interval or a maintenance window rather than more retries.

Groups, tags and maintenance windows

Use groups to mirror how you think about the lab:

  • Infrastructure: Proxmox, the firewall, DNS
  • Home: Home Assistant, the MQTT broker
  • Apps: everything users open

A group shows down when any child is down, so the overview reads at a glance.

Maintenance windows silence notifications for a set of monitors during planned work. Create a recurring one for your monthly update hour, so the planned reboot of the Proxmox host does not page you.

Jobs that run on a schedule: push monitors

For backups and cron jobs, a push monitor turns the check around: Uptime Kuma waits for the job to call a unique URL and goes down if no call arrives in time. For a nightly job, set the interval slightly longer than the schedule (the book uses 25 hours) and call the URL at the end of the job, only on success:

curl -fsS -m 10 --retry 3 "$PUSH?status=up&msg=OK"

With set -e at the top of the script, a failing step ends it before the curl, the heartbeat never arrives, and the monitor goes down. Silence is the failure signal.

Who watches the watcher?

If the monitoring guest dies, its own Uptime Kuma cannot tell you. The book closes that gap with two small moves:

  1. Run a second Uptime Kuma on separate hardware (a Raspberry Pi or any always-on machine) with a handful of monitors: the monitoring guest, the Proxmox web interface on port 8006, the router.
  2. Add a Push monitor on that second instance and have the monitoring guest call it every minute from cron:
# crontab -e on the monitoring guest
* * * * * curl -fsS -m 10 -o /dev/null http://192.168.10.5:3001/api/push/Wd9Kq2

If the guest, its host or its network goes away, the pushes stop and the second instance alerts. (The address and push token are the book's example lab; use the URL your own push monitor shows.)

Notifications and a status page

Add a notification once under Settings, then Notifications, and attach it to many monitors. The book uses ntfy (its next chapter) and ticks "Default enabled" so new monitors get it automatically.

A status page shows chosen monitors without a login. Add only the family-facing services and it answers "is it just me?" for everyone in the house. Keep it on the internal network: publishing it on the internet tells strangers what you run.

Checklist

  • Uptime Kuma 2 running from a Compose file, data on local disk
  • A keyword monitor for every web app; TCP or DNS monitors for the rest
  • Retries set to 2 with a 20 s retry interval; certificate expiry on for HTTPS
  • Groups for Infrastructure, Home and Apps, plus a recurring maintenance window
  • Push monitors on every backup and scheduled job
  • A second watcher on separate hardware with a dead-man push from the monitoring guest
  • One default notification and an internal-only status page

Go deeper: Watch Your Homelab

item.title: Free 3D-printed HC-SR501 PIR sensor case with a rim clip (STL download)
item.description: A free 3D-printed case for the HC-SR501 PIR motion sensor with a snap-on lid and a sawtooth clip that grips a 9.7 to 11.5 mm tank or tote rim. STL and OpenSCAD downloads, the exact ABS print settings, and the real print timelapse.
item.content:encoded:
The HC-SR501 is the cheap PIR motion sensor in a lot of DIY builds, and it usually ends up taped or zip-tied somewhere. This is a free case for it that clips straight onto the rim of a tank or tote: the board slides in, a lid snaps on, and a sawtooth U-clip underneath grips the rim. It was designed for a turtle tote whose rim measured 9.5 to 10.2 mm, and the OpenSCAD source is included so the clip can be changed for a different rim.

Printed and assembled

The photos here are the real case, printed in ABS, with an HC-SR501 inside and clipped onto the tote. The lens dome looks out through the front window, and the three Dupont wires come out of the slot in the back.

Downloads

  • turtle_pir_case_body_print.stl (163 KB): the case body with the clip, already oriented for printing
  • turtle_pir_case_lid_print.stl (76 KB): the snap-on lid
  • turtle_pir_case.scad: the editable OpenSCAD source
  • abs_raft_profile.ini: the PrusaSlicer profile the case was sliced with
  • Everything as one zip

Also on Printables. License: CC BY 4.0, Charles Hartmann / Homelab the Right Way.

What it fits

The standard HC-SR501 board: a 32.5 x 24 mm PCB, a 23 mm lens dome that stands 15 mm off the board, the 3-pin header on one long edge and the two trim pots on the other. The board slides down into slots in the side walls (2.0 mm slots for the 1.6 mm board), header edge up, with the Dupont plugs already on.

The case

  • Size: 37.6 x 20.8 x 32 mm with the lid, 51 mm tall including the clip. 2.2 mm walls, 2.5 mm floor, 2.0 mm front.
  • Front: a 24.2 mm window for the dome, which sticks out about 8.5 mm. A 1.6 mm outer chamfer keeps the wall from shading the dome's side view. The window is open to the top as a slot so the board can slide in with its dome on; a tongue on the lid closes it.
  • Back: an 11 x 9.5 mm U-slot for the three Dupont plugs (they stick out about 4 mm), and a 22 x 6 mm screwdriver window over both trim pots. Sensitivity and delay can be adjusted with the case closed.
  • Lid: two 1.0 x 5 mm legs with 0.5 mm bumps click into grooves in the side walls (about 0.3 mm of interference). Two tabs on the lid hold the board down.

The clip

The clip is a U under the floor that runs the full 37.6 mm width of the case. Each jaw is 19.05 mm (0.75 in) long and 3.5 mm thick, with a 1.2 mm lead-in at the tip. The gap is 11.5 mm at the root, and each jaw has 6 sawtooth teeth, 0.9 mm tall on a 2.4 mm pitch, with the steep catch face up and the shallow ramp down. That leaves 9.7 mm between the tooth tips, so it grips rims about 9.7 to 11.5 mm thick: it slides on easily and bites when pulled up.

Print settings that worked

The case in the photos was printed in ABS with these settings (they are in abs_raft_profile.ini):

  • Nozzle 240 °C, bed 100 °C
  • 0.2 mm layers, 0.4 mm nozzle, 4 perimeters, 40 percent gyroid infill
  • Raft: 3 layers, 0.2 mm contact gap, 1.5 mm expansion. No brim, no skirt.
  • No supports. The body prints upright with the jaw tips on the bed; the only bridges are the 11.5 mm floor between the jaws and the top of the pot window. The lid prints top face down.
  • Body and lid fit on one plate: 248 layers. PrusaSlicer estimated 2 h 50 min and about 16 g of ABS (15.3 cm³, 6.37 m of filament). The real print took about 3 h 08 min on OctoPrint.

Assembly

  1. Plug your three Dupont jumpers onto the sensor's header.
  2. Slide the board down into the side slots, dome toward the front window, header edge up. The plugs come out through the back slot.
  3. Press the lid on until it clicks.
  4. Push the clip straight down over the rim.

Changing it (OpenSCAD)

The adjustable values are at the top of turtle_pir_case.scad. Edit, press F6, export the STL (part = "print_body" or "print_lid" gives the print-oriented parts).

  • gap: jaw face to jaw face at the root, 11.5 mm. Measure your rim and set it a little over the thickness.
  • tooth_h, tooth_p: tooth height (0.9 mm) and pitch (2.4 mm).
  • jaw_len: how far the jaws reach below the floor, 19.05 mm.
  • clr: board side clearance, 0.35 mm.
  • pcb_w, pcb_h, lens_d: the board and dome size, from the HC-SR501 datasheet.

The design was drawn in OpenSCAD with AI help, from the HC-SR501 datasheet dimensions.

item.title: D4 is GPIO6: the six XIAO ESP32-C3 pins the tank build uses, and their two names
item.description: The Smart Turtle Tank water sensor touches only six pins on the XIAO ESP32-C3. Here is what each one does, why the signal pins are D1, D2 and D4, and the naming trap that bites when you move from Arduino code to ESPHome.
item.content:encoded:
The water sensor in Smart Turtle Tank uses a Seeed XIAO ESP32-C3 and exactly six of its pins: 5V, GND, 3V3, D1, D2 and D4. Those names are printed right on the board next to each pin, which makes the wiring easy to check by eye. The trap is that the chip underneath does not call them that. Your sketch says D4, your ESPHome file says GPIO6, and they are the same pin. Mix the two naming systems up and a perfectly wired build reads nothing.

This post is a tour of the six pins: what each one is for, why the build picked it, and how to name it in each place you will type it.

Two names for every signal pin

The book's glossary puts it in one line: a GPIO is a general-purpose pin on the chip; the XIAO labels them D0 to D10, and the chip numbers them differently. D4 is GPIO6.

Which name works depends on where you type it:

  • On the board and in the wiring steps: the printed labels. D1, D2, D4.
  • In the PlatformIO sketch: also the labels, because the project picks the board. board = seeed_xiao_esp32c3 is what makes D1, D2 and D4 mean the right pins. With a different board name, D4 means a different pin.
  • In ESPHome YAML: the chip's numbers. The book's Home Assistant chapter writes the same pin map as GPIO6, GPIO3 and GPIO4, each with a comment saying which D label it is.

The same three pins, written both ways:

XIAO labelChip pinGoes toSketchESPHome
D4GPIO6DS18B20 DAT (adapter has the 4.7 kΩ pull-up)TEMP_PIN D4pin: GPIO6
D1GPIO3 (ADC1)TDS board ATDS_PIN D1pin: GPIO3
D2GPIO4 (ADC1)Turbidity S through the ÷5 dividerTURB_PIN D2pin: GPIO4

The habit that saves you: every time you write a chip number, put the label next to it in a comment, the way the book does.

#define TEMP_PIN D4        // GPIO6, DS18B20 DAT (adapter has the pull-up)
#define TDS_PIN D1         // GPIO3, ADC1
#define TURB_PIN D2        // GPIO4, ADC1, through the /5 divider module
one_wire:
  - platform: gpio
    pin: GPIO6            # XIAO D4
  - platform: adc
    pin: GPIO3            # XIAO D1, TDS board A

The three power pins

5V is the USB supply passed straight through. Exactly one wire goes to it in the whole build: the turbidity board's V. The book's jumper colours make it the only red jumper in the build (the sensors' own cables have their own colours, so go by the printed letters).

3V3 is regulated down for the chip. The temperature adapter and the TDS board both run from it, which keeps their signals under the chip's limit. The book's common mistake here is plugging a sensor into 5V "because it is more power": more volts in means more volts out, and the signal pin is what pays for it.

GND is ground, the minus side, and every board's GND connects to every other's. The XIAO has exactly one GND pin and one 3V3 pin while four boards need each of them, which is why the breadboard is in the parts list at all. One jumper from GND to the breadboard's − line and one from 3V3 to the + line turn those rows into power strips. A strip of tape by the + line that says "3V3, not 5V" is part of the build.

Why D1 and D2 carry the analog probes

The TDS board and the turbidity divider both output a voltage, so they need pins wired to the ADC, the part of the XIAO that turns a voltage on a pin into a number. D1 (GPIO3) and D2 (GPIO4) are both on ADC1, and that is deliberate: on an ESP32, ADC2 stops working while Wi-Fi is on, and ADC1 does not. Move a probe to an ADC2 pin and it stops reading as soon as the firmware brings Wi-Fi up.

The firmware reads them with analogReadMilliVolts(), which applies the chip's factory calibration and returns millivolts. At the default attenuation that reads accurately up to about 2.5 V, and the chip's inputs can only take 3.3 V at all. That is why the turbidity board, which runs on 5 V and outputs up to 4.5 V, never goes straight into D2: its S wire goes into a ÷5 divider and D2 reads the divider's output, so 4.5 V arrives as 0.9 V. The code multiplies by TURB_RATIO 5.0f (or 2.0f with the two-resistor ÷2 divider) to get the sensor's real voltage back.

Why D4 carries the temperature probe

D4 is not on that list because it does not need the ADC. The DS18B20 is a digital sensor that talks over a single wire using 1-Wire, sending the temperature as a number rather than a voltage. That is why it is the accurate one, ±0.5 °C out of the box, with no calibration maths. The data line needs a pull-up resistor; the adapter board already has the 4.7 kΩ one, so nothing gets added between D4 and DAT.

One thing D4 can still send you that looks like data: the Dallas library returns -127 when the probe is not connected and 85.0 at power-on. Both versions of the firmware throw those away. In ESPHome:

      filters:
        - filter_out: 85.0
        - filter_out: -127.0

Before the USB cable goes in

The book's power-up check is written against these six pins. With USB unplugged:

  • The − line has six wires: XIAO GND, temp GND, TDS −, turbidity G, divider GND terminal, divider −.
  • The + line has three wires: XIAO 3V3, temp VCC, TDS +. Nothing from 5V.
  • Only one wire on 5V: to turbidity V.
  • Turbidity S goes to the divider, not to the XIAO. D2 connects to the divider's S pin.
  • Signals: D4 to temp DAT, D1 to TDS A, D2 to divider S.
  • The turbidity board's switch is on A.

Then plug in. Nothing should get warm and nothing should smell; if it does, unplug and recheck the 5V and GND wires. And keep the cable out until the last wire is in: plugging it in "just to see the light" means every later wire goes onto a live board.

Checklist

  • Wire by the printed labels; go by the letters on each sensor board, not the cable colours.
  • In the sketch, keep board = seeed_xiao_esp32c3 so D1, D2 and D4 mean what the wiring means.
  • In ESPHome, write GPIO6, GPIO3 and GPIO4, each with its D label in a comment.
  • Analog probes only on ADC1 pins (D1 and D2 here), never ADC2, because Wi-Fi is on.
  • Nothing over 3.3 V into a D pin; the turbidity signal goes through the divider.
  • One red wire on 5V, three wires on the + line, six on the − line, then USB last.
